value: auditory evoked potential responses between 30 and 500 Hz, lowest thresholds between 100 and 200 Hz
method: auditory evoked potential (AEP) recording from sedated squid; amplitude-modulated tone-pips (at least six cycles) from an underwater speaker in a tank, with a separate shaker setup delivering single-cycle acceleration impulses masked by tones; pressure and particle motion both measured; threshold taken either as the lowest level at which a response could still be seen or from a regression of FFT amplitude at twice the stimulus frequency crossing zero response
conditions: 19 squid in all: 15 for in-vivo tank recordings and 4 for shaker recordings; mantle length mean 14.8 +/- 3.1 cm (+/- not defined in the text read), wet mass 54.7 +/- 18.9 g; sedated in a magnesium chloride bath (a drug effect on the squid's response cannot be excluded), held ventral side up near the surface in acoustically transparent mesh (tank) or resting in a bowl under a thin layer of seawater (shaker); full audiograms were not collected from every animal; example visually determined threshold 101 dB re 1 uPa rms at 100 Hz from a single animal, and a best acceleration threshold of -26 dB re 1 m s-2 in the shaker; pressure in dB re 1 uPa (rms), acceleration in dB re 1 m s-2; tested frequency range and the upper limit of the 30 to 500 Hz band (whether a test ceiling or a response limit) not established from the text read; best frequency about 100 to 300 Hz; the authors conclude the detected component is particle motion, not pressure; no control recordings (dead animal, electrode moved) were checked in the text read

value: a response was recorded for 67% of looms, 50% of overhead passes and 35% of blank-screen controls
method: freely moving animals in a small tank (15 x 25 x 15 cm) under a backlit screen shown an expanding dark disc (loom, 10 to 70 deg over 0.5 s), an overhead pass (70 deg circle moving across the screen) or a blank white screen; response (sudden jerks of the arms or raising of the dorsal-most spines) scored from video by five blind observers; Bayesian model with stimulus type fixed and animal and observer random
conditions: 14 wild-collected adults (Isla Solarte, Panama), 3-day recovery in open-air aquaria; 36 videos scored: 14 looms, 14 overhead passes and 8 blank-screen controls; animals exposed to each stimulus only once, 4 min habituation between stimuli; response timing not recorded; the 35% response rate to blank screens means the response is not specific to the moving stimuli, and the percentages cannot be whole-video counts (67% of 14 is not an integer), so they are probably pooled over the five observers (70 scorings per moving stimulus, 40 for controls; my inference, not stated in the quote); the model reported in the following Results sentence put the probability of a response above control at over 99% for looms and 96% for overhead passes (read from the fetch summary, not the quoted sentence); daytime irradiance in the size experiments was 379 +/- 291 W m-2 (not measured for the loom tank)

conditions: treatment light-strep: neuromasts made non-functional with streptomycin (5 mmol/l; drug side effects on other systems not tested in the text read), tested in light (30 uE m-2 s-1), so vision alone; N = 61 larvae in this treatment (per size-class N not given); the range is across size classes with no ontogenetic change (P = 0.26) and a slope different from light-control larvae (P = 0.002); comparison groups in the same Results section: dark-strep (neither neuromast nor visual input, N = 90) responded in 0 to 7% (fetch summary of a longer sentence), and light-control larvae (N = 89) rose from 57% at 5 to 7 mm TL to 100% at 20 mm; lab-reared larvae from NMFS Beaufort Laboratory embryos, 20 to 22 C, salinity 29 to 31 per mille; larvae not stated to be reused; response to the probe does not separate vision from any residual non-neuromast sense, and the probe was approached by hand
